```{r, include=FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readxl)
library(httr)
library(rvest)

```



<!-- Feel free to modify the subsection names -->


# Data

The CIA World Factbook provides basic intelligence on the history, people, government, economy, energy,
geography, environment, communications, transportation, military, terrorism, and transnational issues for
266 world entities.

In this case study you will work with world data from 2020 which contains information on

- median age
- youth unemployment rate
- net migration rate (difference between the number of persons entering and leaving a country during the year per 1,000 persons - based on midyear population)

for most world entities. The data was downloaded from https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/about/archives/.
For data manipulation, `dplyr` functions should be used. For importing data, any package can be used.


# Tasks

## a) Data loading
<!-- Load in R the following data sets which you can find in TUWEL. For each data set, ensure that missing
values are read in properly, that column names are unambiguous. Each data set should contain at the end
only two columns: country and the variable.
- rawdata_343.txt which contains the (estimated) median age per country. Pay attention! The delimiter
is 2 or more white spaces (one space would not work as it would separate country names which contain
a space); you have to skip the first two lines. Hint: you can look into function read.fwf or the readr
corresponding function. It might also be useful to use tidyr functions to unite some columns back or
separate them.
- rawdata_373.csv which contains the (estimated) youth unemployment rate (15-24) per country
- rawdata_347.txt which contains (estimated) net migration rate per country. -->
```{r, message=FALSE}
data343_location <- "../data/rawdata_343.txt"
data373_location <- "../data/rawdata_373.csv"
data347_location <- "../data/rawdata_347.txt"

# Load data
# Define the widths of the fields
pos343 <- fwf_positions(start = c(9, 75), end = c(74, 79))
pos347 <- fwf_positions(start = c(9, 72), end = c(71, 79))

# Read files into dataframes
rawdata_343 <- read_fwf(data343_location, col_positions = pos343)
rawdata_373 <- read_csv(data373_location)
rawdata_347 <- read_fwf(data347_location, col_positions = pos347)
# Drop first 2 rows
rawdata_343 <- rawdata_343[-c(1, 2), ]
rawdata_347 <- rawdata_347[-c(1, 2), ]

# Set the column names
colnames(rawdata_343) <- c("country_name", "median_age")
colnames(rawdata_347) <- c("country_name", "net_migration_rate")
```

## b) Merging datasets
<!-- Merge the data sets containing raw data using dplyr function on the unique keys. Keep the union of all
observations in the tables. What key are you using for merging? Return the dimension of the merged data
set. -->
```{r}
# Merge the data sets
rawdata <- merge(rawdata_343, rawdata_347, by = "country_name", all = TRUE)
rawdata <- merge(rawdata, rawdata_373, by = "country_name", all = TRUE)

# Return the dimension of the merged data set
print(dim(rawdata))
```


## c) External info extraction
<!-- You will acquire more country level information such as the classification of the country based on income.
Such an information can be found at https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/articles/906519.
From there extract the classification for 2020 into low/lower-middle/upper-middle/high income countries. -->
```{r, message=FALSE}
# Read the xlsx file
income_classification <- read_excel("../data/OGHIST.xlsx", sheet = "Country Analytical History")
# Extract relevant information. That is:
# All elements from the 11th row and the column which at the 5th row has value 2020
# And the respective country name, which is on the 2nd column
country_classification <- income_classification[11:228, c(1, 2, which(income_classification[5, ] == 2020))]
colnames(country_classification) <- c("country_code", "country_name", "income_status")
```


## d) Merging yet again
<!-- Merge this information to the data set in b.
1. What are the common variables? Can you merge using them? Why or why not?
2. A reliable merging for countries are ISO codes as they are standardized across data sources. Download the
mapping of ISO codes to countries from https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/references/country-data-codes/ 
and load it into R.
3. Merge the data sets using the ISO codes. -->
```{r, message=FALSE}
# Merge the data sets
rawdata_wrong <- merge(rawdata, country_classification, by = "country_name", all = TRUE)

# Load country codes
raw_ccodes <- read_csv("../data/Country Data Codes.csv")

# Join raw_ccodes by Name with rawdata by country_name
# From raw_ccode, get only GENC column
rawdata <- left_join(rawdata, raw_ccodes[, c("Name", "GENC")], by = c("country_name" = "Name"))

# Now join can be done by country_code
rawdata <- left_join(rawdata, country_classification[, c("country_code", "income_status")], by = c("GENC" = "country_code"))
```

## e) More external info introduction
<!-- Introduce into the data set information on continent for each country and subcontinent (region). You should
find a way to gather this data. You can find an appropriate online resource, download the data and merge
the information with the existing data set. Name the merged data set df_vars. -->
```{r, message=FALSE}
continent_table_web <- "https://statisticstimes.com/geography/countries-by-continents.php"

# Read the html
response <- httr::GET(continent_table_web) 
continent_table <- content(response, as="text") %>%
  rvest::read_html() %>%
  rvest::html_nodes("#table_id") %>%
  rvest::html_table(na.strings = "")
# Extract to a table
continent_table <- continent_table[[1]]

# Add information of continent, region and sub-region to the rawdata
# Join by ISO-alpha3 Code and GENC
df_vars <- left_join(rawdata, continent_table[, c("ISO-alpha3 Code", "Continent", "Region 1", "Region 2")], by = c("GENC" = "ISO-alpha3 Code"))
```


## f) Discuss tidyness
<!-- Discuss on the tidyness of the data set df_vars. What are the observational 
units, what are the variables?
What can be considered fixed vs measured variables? Tidy the data if needed. -->
It can be said that the dataframe is already tidy. This is because each row represents 
a country and each column represents a variable. Variables are the country name, 
median age, net migration rate, youth unemployment rate, income status classification, 
continent, region and sub-region. The observational units, or samples, are the countries. 
All *fixed* variables are categorical. They are: <u>country_name</u>, <u>GENC</u>, 
<u>Continent</u>, <u>Region 1</u> and <u>Region 2</u>. The measured variables are 
<u>median_age</u>, <u>net_migration_rate</u>, <u>youth_unempl_rate</u> and <u>income_status</u>.
